doc.summary: bootdefs.h - centralized configuration for the MiniOS two-stage boot path.
VESA BIOS Extensions (VBE) linear-framebuffer video setup.
doc.description: Stage 2 probes a true-color mode whose framebuffer fits the emulated std-VGA ~2 MB scan-out window (800x600x32, then 640x480x32), then the 8-bit-palette modes, and records the result for the kernel in a fixed low-memory struct (see VBE_INFO_ADDR). If no VBE mode is available it falls back to VGA Mode 13h (320x200x8). In a true-color mode the kernel expands its palette-index drawing to RGB and the desktop/icon pixels are no longer quantized; the 8-bit modes keep the 256-entry VGA DAC palette path unchanged. A true-color mode taller than 800x600 (1024x768x24 = 2.25 MB) would render its bottom rows black because QEMU only scans out the first ~2 MB of the framebuffer, so none is offered.

doc.summary: Framebuffer info handed to the kernel.
doc.description: Stage 2 writes this fixed low-memory struct; the kernel reads it once at boot to map the linear framebuffer into the user window. Layout: +0  dword  physical base of the linear framebuffer +4  word   bytes per scanline (pitch) +6  word   width in pixels +8  word   height in pixels +10 byte   valid (1 when stage 2 programmed a video mode) +11 byte   bits per pixel (8, 24 or 32; 8 when stage 2 fell back to VGA Mode 13h, whose mode info carries no bpp field)

The SB16 DMA audio ring [0x90000, 0x94000) is read by the 8237 DMA controller directly from physical RAM, bypassing the CPU caches.
doc.description: Those pages must be marked uncacheable (PCD) or the freshly written PCM stays stale in a write-back cache and the DMA plays garbage.

doc.summary: PT0 entry index
Both bits are required for a device mapping: PCD alone leaves the page write-back, so a device writing a status register leaves a stale copy in cache and a poll loop never observes the update.
PDPT slot 4 is the kernel's device-MMIO window (see progs/minios_abi.h MINIOS_DEV_MMIO_VBASE).
doc.description: Slot 0 is the boot identity map, slot 1 the user window, slot 3 the local APIC, and nothing else claims slot 4: it starts at 4 GB of virtual address, above every heap and every ring-3 window.

doc.summary: Dedicated zone for the kernel-installed 4 KB user-window page tables.
doc.description:
It must never share memory with the heap: the ramdisk data area is heap-backed and its size is discovered at boot, so page tables there could be overwritten by a later reservation.

It must ALSO never share memory with the kernel image. The kernel .bss is
~1.4 MB and grows, so a zone placed "between the kernel image and the
user window" (the historical 0x300000) sits right where the kernel's
own .bss lands once the image outgrows 2 MB. That collision silently
corrupted the page tables every time the shell wrote a terminal line
(the line buffer lived in the .bss tail), which is why user programs
crashed intermittently at "unmapped" addresses. The zone therefore
lives at 0x10000, BELOW the kernel link base (0x100000), inside the
boot staging buffer that is dead once the kernel is running: nothing in
the kernel image can ever reach it, in the plain build or under KASLR.
It is identity-mapped in every build (PT0 low half in KASLR, 2 MB PD
leaf in the plain build), so the PDEs can carry the same addresses the
kernel writes through.

doc.summary: KASLR: the kernel image is loaded at a random 2 MB-aligned physical base chosen from a 64-position window above the kernel heap, so the kernel's physical location varies on every boot.
doc.description: The virtual base stays at the link-time address (0x100000); the loader maps it to the chosen physical base. The image (code + .bss) is mapped CONTIGUOUSLY over the whole virtual span [0x100000, KASLR_IMAGE_SPAN): PT0 covers the first MB and PT1 covers [0x200000, KASLR_IMAGE_SPAN) at 4 KB granularity, so a growing .bss can never spill onto the identity-mapped low-memory reserved zones. Keep KASLR_IMAGE_SPAN in sync with the kernel link layout: the image must end below the user window at USER_LOAD_BASE (0x400000).

doc.summary: RAM above 16 MB in 64 KB units (PC BIOS / QEMU convention).
